title: A solver that repeats itself

blocks.text: A cooperative's planning service must give the same answer when an auditor reruns a past solve. The model does not matter here; the solver settings do.

Write `repeatable_solver(seed, work)` in `repeatable.py`. Return a `cp_model.CpSolver` set up so that solving the same model twice, on the same OR-Tools version, gives the same status, objective, counts and plan every time: use `seed` as the random seed and stop after `work` units of deterministic time.
Think about which settings make a run depend on the machine or on the clock, and leave every one of them out. About four lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from ortools.sat.python import cp_model


def repeatable_solver(seed: int, work: float) -> cp_model.CpSolver:
    """A CP-SAT solver whose every count repeats run to run: one worker, a seed, a work limit."""
    solver = cp_model.CpSolver()
    solver.parameters.num_workers = 1
    solver.parameters.random_seed = seed
    solver.parameters.max_deterministic_time = work
    return solver


if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = cp_model.CpModel()
    x = [model.new_bool_var(f"x{i}") for i in range(6)]
    model.add(sum((i + 2) * v for i, v in enumerate(x)) <= 10)
    model.maximize(sum((i + 3) * v for i, v in enumerate(x)))
    solver = repeatable_solver(7, 1.0)
    print(solver.status_name(solver.solve(model)), solver.objective_value)

from ortools.sat.python import cp_model

from repeatable import repeatable_solver

# Eight hedge-cutting jobs, (value, hours), and 30 hours of crew time.
jobs = [(40, 9), (25, 6), (33, 8), (18, 4), (29, 7), (12, 3), (36, 10), (21, 5)]


def solve(seed, work):
    model = cp_model.CpModel()
    pick = [model.new_bool_var(f"job{i}") for i in range(len(jobs))]
    model.add(sum(h * p for (_, h), p in zip(jobs, pick)) <= 30)
    model.maximize(sum(v * p for (v, _), p in zip(jobs, pick)))
    solver = repeatable_solver(seed, work)
    status = solver.solve(model)
    return solver, (solver.status_name(status), solver.objective_value, solver.num_branches, solver.num_conflicts)


solver, first = solve(9, 1.0)
_, second = solve(9, 1.0)
print("workers, seed, work limit:", solver.parameters.num_workers, solver.parameters.random_seed,
      solver.parameters.max_deterministic_time)
print("seed 9, first run (status, objective, branches, conflicts):", first)
print("seed 9, second run:", second)

cases.says: the solver runs one worker with the seed it was given
two solves of the same model agree on status, objective, branches, conflicts and values
the limit is the given amount of deterministic work, and no wall-clock limit is set

origin.section: A Wall-Clock Limit Stops the Search at a Different Point Each Run

concepts: one worker, a fixed seed and a deterministic work limit make every count of a run repeat
